questions.question: When is a metric space $(\boldsymbol{X},d)$ called complete?
options: Every sequence contained in it is Cauchy.
No sequence in it converges.
Every point is at distance $1$ from every other point.
Every Cauchy sequence in it converges in $(\boldsymbol{X},d)$.

questions.question: Which interpretation best describes a complete metric space?
options: It contains no convergent sequence at all, so no limit can ever lie outside the space.
It has no missing points for Cauchy sequences to converge to outside the space.
It makes every subset compact.
It removes the need for a metric.

questions.question: What does the completion of a metric space guarantee for Cauchy sequences?
options: Every Cauchy sequence converges in the completion.
No Cauchy sequence converges in the completion.
Only the constant sequences exist in the completion.
The metric is no longer used in the completion.

questions.question: A metric space contains a Cauchy sequence that does not converge in that space. What can be concluded?
options: The metric space is complete by definition.
The metric space is not complete.
The sequence cannot be Cauchy.
The space must equal $\mathbb{R}^n$.

questions.question: Suppose $(\boldsymbol{X},d)$ is complete and $(\boldsymbol{x}_n)$ is Cauchy in $\boldsymbol{X}$. What follows?
options: $(\boldsymbol{x}_n)$ must leave $\boldsymbol{X}$.
$(\boldsymbol{x}_n)$ cannot have a limit in $\boldsymbol{X}$.
$(\boldsymbol{x}_n)$ must be finite.
$(\boldsymbol{x}_n)$ converges in $(\boldsymbol{X},d)$.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes being Cauchy from completeness?
options: Cauchy is a property of a metric space, while completeness is a property of one single point.
Cauchy is a property of a sequence, while completeness is a property of the metric space.
They are the same property with different names.
Completeness is defined without reference to Cauchy sequences.

questions.question: Which missing condition makes the statement “a Cauchy sequence converges” valid?
options: The sequence is written with bold symbols.
The radius is positive.
The set is an open cover.
The surrounding metric space is complete.

questions.question: A normed vector space is complete. Which term can be used for it?
options: Banach space
Exterior point
Open metric ball
Boundary of a set

questions.question: In a complete metric space, a sequence “looks like it should converge” because it is Cauchy. What must happen?
options: It must have a missing limit outside the space.
It becomes an open cover.
It stops being a sequence.
It lands at a limit inside the space.

questions.question: In a complete metric space, where must the limit of every Cauchy sequence in $X$ lie?
options: Outside $X$.
Only in the completion but never in $X$.
In every metric space at once.
Inside the same metric space $X$.

questions.question: Which object is complete or incomplete for completeness?
options: A metric space.
A single real number.
An open cover.
A finite subcover.

questions.question: Let $(V,\|\cdot\|)$ be a real normed vector space, and let $d$ be a complete metric on $V$. Which condition makes completeness of $d$ directly prove that $V$ is Banach for the given norm?
options: The metric $d$ is bounded on $V\times V$.
$d(\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{v})=\|\boldsymbol{u}-\boldsymbol{v}\|$ for all $\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{v}\in V$.
$d(\boldsymbol{u}+\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{v}+\boldsymbol{w})=d(\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{v})$ for all vectors.
$d(\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{v})\ge\|\boldsymbol{u}-\boldsymbol{v}\|$ for all vectors.

questions.question: Suppose $(X,d)$ is complete and $(x_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence in $X$. Which statement is true?
options: $(x_n)$ cannot converge in $X$.
There is some $x\in X$ such that $x_n\to x$.
$(x_n)$ must eventually leave $X$.
$(x_n)$ converges, but possibly to a point outside $X$.

questions.question: A complete normed vector space $V$ is given. Which name may be used for $V$?
options: Compact set
Open cover
Banach space
Punctured neighbourhood

questions.question: Which example fits the statement that a space has no missing points for Cauchy sequences?
options: Every sequence in $X$ is eventually constant.
Every sequence in $X$ diverges.
Every point of $X$ is isolated, and every Cauchy sequence in $X$ fails to converge to any point of $X$.
Every Cauchy sequence in $X$ converges to a point of $X$.

questions.question: Which statement is not implied by completeness alone?
options: Every sequence in the space converges.
Every Cauchy sequence in the space converges in the space.
A complete normed vector space is a Banach space.
Cauchy sequences have no missing limit points inside the space.
